- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 1–3% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >5% from prior day), model should not overreact — cap forecast slope to avoid overshoot; reduce rate of increase by 10–20%.
- If official event net is bearish (net < -10) and sentiment is neutral or bearish, model should not ignore downward pressure — shift forecast mean 2–5% lower than baseline.
- In high-event periods (≥20 events/30d), model should not assume linear continuation — introduce slight downward bias (–1–2%) to reflect supply/demand imbalance.
- If sentiment history shows repeated bearish swings (e.g., -0.5 to -1.0) followed by recovery, model should not overcorrect — allow 1–2 day lag in reversal to avoid premature peak.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral, model should not overfit to recent highs — use 3–5 day moving average to smooth out noise.
- In low-event periods (≤15 events/30d), model should not assume sustained trend — allow 1–2% downward drift to reflect mean reversion.
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome (e.g., 3–5% gap over 30d), adjust upward by 1–2% per day to reflect sentiment-driven rally.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome (e.g., 3–5% gap over 30d), adjust downward by 1–2% per day to reflect sentiment-driven correction.
- In high-event, bearish sentiment context, model should not ignore policy or supply shocks — reduce forecast by 2–5% for each major auction or policy event.
